extracted.intended_audience: students, faculty, staff, school administrators, and potential clients seeking legal guidance on Title IX compliance and proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining the practical and legal consequences of the Department of Education reverting enforcement to the 2020 Title IX Rule, and what complainants, respondents, and institutions must change or expect in investigations and adjudications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five enforcement focus areas (Department guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department specifically highlighted five issues to be enforced under the 2020 Title IX Rule: the definition of sexual harassment; procedural protections for complainants and respondents; provision of supportive measures for complainants; reporting processes at the school level; and the interpretation of 'sex'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list frames the main regulatory topics institutions should review and update immediately; each of the five areas is discussed separately in the guidance and in this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sexual harassment (2020 Rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment is defined to include three broad types of sexual misconduct: (1) quid pro quo harassment by an employee of an educational institution; (2) unwelcome offensive conduct that denies access to equal education opportunities; and (3) sexual violence or assault (as defined under certain federal statutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the 2020 Rule, actionable harassment requires unwelcome conduct that a reasonable person would find so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it denies a person equal educational access. Institutions must apply this 'severe and pervasive' standard (both prongs required) and the conduct must effectively deny equal access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severe-and-pervasive standard (contrast with 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be actionable under Title IX (per 2020 Rule) unwelcome offensive conduct must be both severe and pervasive and must effectively prevent the complainant from obtaining equal access to educational programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with the 2024 Rule attempt to treat conduct as harassment if it was either severe or pervasive (not both) and to treat conduct as harassment if it merely 'limited' rather than 'denied' equal access. Because 2024 is unenforceable under the Department’s guidance, apply the 2020 dual prong test and the 'denial of equal access' threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live hearing requirement for post-secondary institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 rules require colleges and universities to include provisions in their grievance processes that provide for a live hearing to determine responsibility for a Title IX violation, with advisors permitted to cross-examine the other party and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearings must be 'live' but parties may be in separate rooms or appear virtually. K-12 schools may offer live hearings but are not required to do so. Because the 2024 Rule’s allowance for less formal adjudication is no longer in force, post-secondary institutions must restore live hearing procedures with cross-examination mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination through advisors
rubrics_metrics.description: During live hearings advisors working with complainants and respondents must be permitted to cross-examine the other party and witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must design the hearing process to allow advisor-conducted cross-examination (including via separate rooms/virtual means) consistent with the 2020 Rule’s protections for respondents and both parties’ procedural rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and evidentiary standard selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 rules required schools to choose one evidentiary standard for all Title IX disciplinary proceedings: either 'clear and convincing evidence' or 'preponderance of the evidence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions provided: 'preponderance' = more likely than not; 'clear and convincing' = 'highly probable.' The rules also specify that both the burden of proof and the burden of gathering evidence rest with the schools rather than the parties. Institutions must adopt one standard uniformly and ensure the institution (not parties) shoulders evidence-gathering responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on single-investigator model
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'single investigator' model is not allowed under the 2020 rules: the person who served as Title IX Coordinator or investigated the complaint may not serve as the decision-maker in the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must separate investigative and decision-making roles to avoid conflicts and preserve impartial adjudication; this was a notable procedural protection introduced in 2020 and reaffirmed by the Department’s guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to appeal for both complainants and respondents
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools are required to offer a process for both complainants and respondents to appeal the decision in a Title IX adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal procedures must be available to both parties and established in institution policy; institutions should ensure appeal decision-makers are impartial and that appeal timelines and grounds are clearly defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on imposing sanctions before grievance process conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools are prohibited from imposing any sanctions on respondents before they have followed the grievance process to a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interim measures that are punitive or effectively sanctions must be avoided prior to final determination; institutions should distinguish supportive interim measures from sanctions to comply with the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: definition and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Supportive measures are 'individualized services reasonably available that are nonpunitive, non-disciplinary, and not unreasonably burdensome to the other party while designed to ensure equal educational access, protect safety, or deter sexual harassment.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive measures must be 'not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances' and provided for free. Examples include offering an extension on a deadline and counseling services. Institutions must balance complainant safety with avoiding unreasonable burdens on respondents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting processes and Title IX Coordinator notification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2020 rules require schools to notify students and employees about contact information for the institution’s Title IX Coordinator and to notify those applying for admission, those applying for employment, parents and guardians of K-12 students, and all unions. Contact information must be displayed 'prominently' on the school's website. Any person can report sexual harassment or other sex discrimination in person, by phone, by mail, or via email.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should ensure prominent, accessible publication of Title IX Coordinator contact info and multiple reporting channels; this enhances notice and accessibility and is a compliance obligation under the 2020 Rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Response obligations: 'prompt' and 'not deliberately indifferent'
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions must respond 'promptly' to reports, and the response need only be 'not deliberately indifferent,' which the rules define as 'not clearly unreasonable in light of the known circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is no set timeframe provided by the Rule; attorneys and courts rely on case law to determine adequacy of response. Institutions should document timely actions and reasonableness assessments to defend against claims of indifference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'sex' under Title IX (2020 interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Dear Colleague letter orders schools to interpret 'sex' as 'the objective, immutable characteristic of being born male or female as outlined in the 2020 Title IX Rule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reverses the Biden Administration's broader interpretive guidance that had included sex stereotypes, sex characteristics, pregnancy/lactation, marital/family/parental status, sexual orientation, and gender identity. Institutions should align policies and adjudications with the 2020 definition unless and until changed by enforceable law or valid future rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive branch and court citations supporting enforcement change
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department cited Executive Order 14168 (directing agencies to enforce sex-based rights protecting men and women as biologically distinct sexes) and a U.S. District Court decision vacating the 2024 Rule as grounds for reverting to the 2020 Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should be aware that the Department’s guidance relies on both executive directives and recent litigation; however, further judicial or appellate action could change the enforceability landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate reorientation of pending investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department announced that any open Title IX investigations that were initiated under the 2024 Rule should be 'immediately reoriented' to comply with the requirements set forth in the 2020 Rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, schools must review ongoing cases and modify procedures, standards, and potential remedies to align with 2020 requirements; this transitional action could give rise to legal challenges from parties to cases that were adjudicated under 2024 standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationwide enforceability determination by the Department of Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting Assistant Secretary stated that the Office for Civil Rights would be enforcing Title IX protections 'under the provisions of the 2020 Title IX Rule, rather than the recently invalidated 2024 Title IX Rule,' making clear that the Department considers the 2024 provisions unenforceable throughout the country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should treat the Department's guidance as the operative enforcement posture until further notice, while monitoring for appellate or other judicial developments that might overturn or modify the Department’s position.
